headline: Zoom flaw allowed remote device takeover, including iPhones and Macs, discovered with AI
summary: A critical vulnerability in Zoom's screen-sharing feature could have allowed attackers to remotely execute code on participants' devices.
details: A newly discovered Zoom vulnerability, aided by an AI tool, allowed an attacker to remotely execute code on a victim's device. This critical flaw could have led to full device takeover, impacting users on platforms like iPhone and Mac.

The vulnerability was specifically tied to Zoom's screen-sharing functionality. Attackers could exploit this bug to gain unauthorized control over other devices participating in a call, posing a significant privacy and security risk.

The discovery highlights the evolving landscape of cybersecurity, where even AI tools are now assisting in uncovering complex software flaws. Zoom has since addressed the issue, urging users to update their applications to the latest version.

headline: Mistral AI wants to build 1 gigawatt of European compute by 2030
summary: Mistral AI aims for 1GW of European compute by 2030, backed by multi-year enterprise commitments. This massive infrastructure project could require an estimated $38 billion in capital expenditure.
details: Mistral AI is pushing for European AI sovereignty, announcing a three-part expansion of its infrastructure business. The French company aims to underwrite 200 megawatts of infrastructure across Europe by the end of 2027, scaling to a full gigawatt by 2030.

The expansion includes regional inference endpoints, allowing customers to choose between European or US AI workloads, and a new "Priority Tier" with an uptime guarantee for critical deployments. A coalition of European enterprises is making multi-year compute commitments to finance this buildout.

In a notable move, Mistral AI will also begin hosting third-party open models on its platform, starting with GLM-5.2 from Z.ai, a Chinese AI lab. This decision may draw scrutiny from those focused on strict European sovereignty.

These announcements signify a shift for Mistral AI, moving beyond its reputation for training open-weight language models to selling critical infrastructure. The company now offers assured capacity, regional control, and contractual reliability for enterprises and governments.

Mistral currently operates less than 200 megawatts of capacity. Near-term plans include a 44-megawatt facility near Paris, a 23-megawatt facility in Sweden built with EcoDataCenter using renewable energy, and a 10-megawatt site in Les Ulis, France.

Reaching one gigawatt by 2030 represents a significant leap in scale. Research firm Epoch AI estimates a typical one-gigawatt AI data center requires roughly $38 billion in upfront capital expenditure, with servers and GPUs accounting for most of the cost.

Mistral's co-founder and CTO, Timothée Lacroix, acknowledged the substantial investment required, stating it necessitates significant scaling and revenue. He highlighted an anticipated supply crunch in AI compute, especially in Europe, expected to worsen around 2027 and 2028.

To finance this, Mistral is assembling an "anchor group" of enterprises whose long-term commitments will collectively fund the infrastructure. These commitments convert into "European Compute Units" (ECUs), a claim on Mistral-built capacity over multiple years for various AI workloads.

This financing structure resembles a power-purchase agreement, reflecting how data center financing is increasingly akin to large infrastructure projects. Mistral previously raised €830 million ($962 million) in debt earlier this year for its Paris data center.
